lead: Unit 6 shows how Python is used beyond single scripts: arrays and tables, scientific and machine-learning libraries, desktop GUIs, threads, and pointer-based data structures. After it you can vectorize numerical work, clean a table, train a simple model, build a Tkinter window, protect shared data with a lock, and implement a linked list, BST and graph traversal.
about: The unit moves from data to interface to concurrency to structures. Chapter 6.1 introduces NumPy arrays and vectorized operations; 6.2 puts the same tabular thinking into Pandas Series and DataFrames. Chapter 6.3 uses SciPy for scientific routines and scikit-learn for a fit/predict workflow. Chapters 6.4 and 6.5 build Tkinter GUIs: widgets first, then layout managers, menus and message boxes. Chapter 6.6 explains threads and synchronization with locks and queues. Chapter 6.7, taught by only a few universities, implements linked lists, binary trees, BSTs and graphs using classes and recursion. The chapters assume functions, classes, files and exceptions from Units 2 to 5, and each later chapter reuses the earlier data or event ideas.

chapters.idea: A NumPy array stores numbers of one type in a fixed shape, and whole-array operations replace Python loops.
chapters.depth: Cover ndarray creation with array, zeros, ones, arange and linspace; attributes shape, ndim, dtype; indexing, slicing and Boolean masks; broadcasting; universal functions such as np.sqrt; reductions with sum, mean, max and axis; reshape and matrix product. Some syllabi call this numerical arrays or vectorised computing. Keep hand-written loop comparisons short.

figure.title: a and a+10
figure.aria: A 2 by 3 array a with rows 1 2 3 and 4 5 6, its elementwise sum with 10, and column sums 5 7 9.

chapters.example: For a = np.array([[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]), give the results of a + 10, a * 2, a.sum(axis=0) and a[:, 1], and state the shape of a. Expected: a + 10 is [[11,12,13],[14,15,16]], a * 2 is [[2,4,6],[8,10,12]], a.sum(axis=0) is [5,7,9], a[:, 1] is [2,5], shape is (2,3).
chapters.trap: The axis=0 reduction works down columns and returns one value per column; it does not sum each row. Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, so (2,3) with (3,) works but (2,) with (3,) does not.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 lists and indexing; Unit 5 modules and packages.
chapters.leave: File loading to 6.2 and Unit 5; random-number generators and advanced linear algebra to later reading.

chapters.idea: Pandas gives labelled one-dimensional Series and two-dimensional DataFrames so selection, cleaning and grouping are table operations.
chapters.depth: Cover Series and DataFrame creation from lists and dictionaries; index and columns; head, info, describe; selection with loc and iloc; Boolean filtering; missing values with isna, fillna, dropna; adding columns; sort_values; groupby; simple merge. Some syllabi call this data frames or data wrangling. Use small tables, not big data.

figure.title: marks DataFrame
figure.aria: A marks table with rows Asha, Bilal and Chen and columns Math, Sci and Total; Total is the row sum.

chapters.example: Given df = pd.DataFrame({'Math':[78,45,90],'Sci':[82,50,88]}, index=['Asha','Bilal','Chen']), add Total = Math + Sci, select rows with Math ≥ 50, and give the mean Total of the selected rows. Expected totals are 160, 95, 178; selected rows are Asha and Chen; their mean Total is 169.
chapters.trap: loc uses labels and includes the end label; iloc uses integer positions and excludes the stop. Avoid chained indexing for assignment; use one loc or direct column assignment.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 dictionaries and lists; 6.1 for column-wise arrays.
chapters.leave: CSV parsing details to Unit 5; plotting and time-series methods to other units.

chapters.idea: SciPy supplies tested scientific functions, and scikit-learn supplies one fit/predict/score interface for many models.
chapters.depth: Cover the role of SciPy for linear algebra, statistics and integration with one example each, such as scipy.linalg.solve and scipy.stats.norm. In scikit-learn cover features X as samples by features, labels y, train_test_split, StandardScaler, a classifier such as KNeighborsClassifier, and fit, predict, score. Some syllabi call this scientific computing and machine-learning basics. Do not derive model mathematics.

figure.title: fit and predict
figure.aria: A scikit-learn pipeline starts with a feature matrix X, splits into train and test, scales features, fits a model, predicts and scores.

chapters.example: Use scipy.linalg.solve for 2x + y = 5 and x + 3y = 6. Then apply sklearn StandardScaler to X = [[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]] and give the transformed first column using population standard deviation. Expected solve: x = 1.8, y = 1.4. First column mean is 3, standard deviation is 1.633, transformed values are about -1.225, 0 and 1.225.
chapters.trap: scikit-learn expects a 2D X of shape samples × features; a 1D list must be reshaped. Fit the scaler on training data only, then transform test data. scipy.linalg.solve needs a square coefficient matrix.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 NumPy arrays; Unit 2 functions; Unit 4 classes and objects for estimator objects.
chapters.leave: Model internals, tuning, deep learning and advanced SciPy subpackages.

chapters.idea: Tkinter builds a GUI as a tree of widget objects under one root window, with callbacks for actions.
chapters.depth: Cover importing Tkinter, one Tk() root, mainloop, and widgets Button, Label, Entry, Checkbutton, Radiobutton, Listbox, Text, Canvas, Frame, Scale, Scrollbar, Spinbox, PanedWindow and LabelFrame. Cover options such as text, command, bg, fg, font, width, height, state and control variables such as StringVar. Show get, insert, delete and event binding. Some syllabi call this GUI widgets or form design.

figure.aria: A Tk root contains a frame with a label, an entry bound to name_var, and a Greet button.

chapters.example: Write Tkinter code that creates a root window, a Label with text 'Name', an Entry bound to a StringVar name_var, and a Button 'Greet' whose command sets a result Label to 'Hello, ' + name_var.get(). After the user types Asha and clicks Greet, what text is shown, and what does name_var.get() return? Expected text is 'Hello, Asha'; get() returns 'Asha'.
chapters.trap: Create exactly one Tk() root and call mainloop(); pass command=greet, not command=greet(). Read Entry text with get(), and keep the control variable alive.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 functions for callbacks; Unit 4 classes and objects because widgets are objects.
chapters.leave: Layout managers, menus and message boxes to 6.5; event-loop internals.

chapters.idea: Geometry managers place widgets in a container, while menus and message boxes add commands and user feedback.
chapters.depth: Cover pack with side, fill, expand; grid with row, column, sticky, padx, pady; place briefly; one manager per container. Cover Menu and Menubutton with add_command and add_cascade, Toplevel windows, and messagebox.showinfo, showwarning and askyesno. Mention standard widget attributes such as relief and border width. Some syllabi call this geometry management or window layout.

figure.title: menu to dialog
figure.aria: A window menu bar leads to a File menu, an Exit item, an askyesno dialog with the question Close?, and then destroy().

chapters.example: Build a window with a File menu. The Exit item calls messagebox.askyesno('Exit','Close?'); if the reply is True, call destroy(). Also place a Label and Entry in a frame with grid: label at row 0 column 0, entry at row 0 column 1. What does askyesno return, and what is the first grid row number? Expected: it returns a Boolean True or False; the first grid row is 0.
chapters.trap: Do not mix pack and grid inside the same master; use one geometry manager per container. askyesno returns a Boolean, not the string 'yes'.
chapters.leave: Widget option catalogue to 6.4; file dialogs and custom dialog classes left out.

chapters.idea: Threads run code concurrently inside one process, and locks or queues stop shared-data races.
chapters.depth: Cover threading.Thread, start, join, daemon threads, and why the GIL does not make compound operations atomic. Cover race conditions, Lock with acquire, release and with, RLock, Semaphore, Event and Condition. Cover queue.Queue for inter-thread communication. Some syllabi call this concurrency or multithreading. Keep OS scheduling theory out.

figure.aria: A main thread starts two worker threads; each acquires a lock, increments a shared counter, releases the lock, and the main thread joins them before reading the final counter.

chapters.example: A shared counter starts at 0. Two threads each run for i in range(100000): counter += 1. Explain why the final value can be less than 200000 without a lock, and give the final value when both increments are inside with lock: counter += 1. Expected: without a lock the read, add and write steps can interleave; with one shared lock the final value is 200000.
chapters.trap: The GIL does not make counter += 1 atomic; it is a read, add and write. Use one shared Lock object and call join() before reading the final counter.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 loops and functions; Unit 4 classes; basic event-loop idea from 6.4-6.5.
chapters.leave: Multiprocessing, async/await, deadlock detection and OS scheduling details.

chapters.idea: Linked lists, trees and graphs store data in nodes joined by references, so size can grow without shifting a Python list.
chapters.depth: Advanced: only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Cover a Node class with data and next for a singly linked list: traversal, insert at head and delete head. Cover binary tree nodes with left and right; binary search tree insert and search; inorder, preorder and postorder traversals. Cover graph representation by adjacency list and BFS/DFS with a visited set. Some syllabi call this linked structures or non-linear data structures.

figure.aria: A binary search tree with root 50, left child 30 with children 20 and 40, and right child 70; inorder gives 20, 30, 40, 50, 70.

chapters.example: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40 into an empty binary search tree in that order. Draw the tree, give the inorder traversal, and search for 40: list the nodes compared. Then build a singly linked list by appending 10, 20, 30 and give the list after deleting the head. Expected inorder: 20, 30, 40, 50, 70; search compares 50, 30, 40; linked list after head deletion is 20 → 30.
chapters.trap: A BST inorder traversal is sorted only if the BST property holds at every node. A graph traversal needs a visited set to avoid cycles. Deleting a linked-list head must update the head reference.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 recursion; Unit 4 classes and objects; Unit 3 lists for adjacency lists.
chapters.leave: Balanced trees, shortest-path algorithms and recursion proof details.

links: NumPy arrays are the input format
Pandas X and y feed fit/predict
widgets are placed by layout managers
long GUI tasks can run in threads
thread and node classes share OOP
